vignette:
Patient Vignette: "The Unfinished Blueprint"

She sits in the chair across from me, her posture perfect—spine straight, hands folded in her lap, the way one might sit through a difficult client meeting. Her name is Amara, and at forty-seven, she has built a career designing spaces that feel safe, that hold people. She is an architect, a partner at a respected firm, and she speaks of her work with a precision that borders on reverence. But when she describes the accident, her voice changes.

It happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. She was driving home from a site visit, her mind still half-occupied with a detail about load-bearing walls. The rain had just started—a sudden, heavy downpour that turned the highway slick. She remembers the way the wipers struggled, the sound of the engine, the smell of wet asphalt. She does not remember the moment of impact, only the aftermath.

A man on a motorcycle had swerved to avoid debris. She didn't see him until he was already there, sliding across her lane. Her car hit him. Not the motorcycle—him. She remembers the thud, a sound she now hears in the quiet moments before sleep. She remembers getting out, the rain soaking through her blouse, the man’s leg bent at an angle that made her stomach drop. She remembers screaming for someone to call an ambulance, remembers the paramedics pushing her aside, remembers the way his eyes fluttered open and then closed.

He survived. But he lost his leg below the knee. She knows this because she called the hospital the next day, and then the next. She knows his name—Marcus. She knows he was a carpenter, that he had two children, that he was on his way to pick up a birthday cake. She has never met him again, but she carries him with her, a ghost in her peripheral vision.

At work, she has become meticulous to the point of paralysis. She checks her blueprints four, five times. She has stopped driving to job sites; she takes the train. She avoids the highway entirely, even if it adds an hour to her commute. Her colleagues have noticed. They ask if she is okay. She says she is fine.

But she is not fine. At night, she lies awake and replays the accident, each time trying to change the ending. What if she had left five minutes later? What if she had taken a different route? What if she had seen him sooner? The questions loop, a broken record in her mind. Her husband, a gentle man who works in IT, reaches for her in bed. She flinches. Not from him, but from the feeling of being touched, of being present in her own body.

She has stopped eating lunch with her team. The break room is too loud, too bright. She eats at her desk, staring at CAD drawings until the lines blur. She has lost twelve pounds. She does not notice.

The guilt is a physical weight. She feels it in her chest, a tightness that makes her breath shallow. She thinks about Marcus constantly. She imagines his life now—the prosthetic, the pain, the birthday cake he never picked up. She wonders if he hates her. She wonders if he thinks of her the way she thinks of him. She has not reached out. She is afraid of what she might hear, or worse, what she might not.

She told me, in our second session, that she used to love driving. She used to roll down the windows and feel the wind on her face. Now, she says, the car feels like a coffin. She has not driven in three months. Her husband drives her everywhere. She thanks him, but she does not look at him when she says it.

She still goes to work. She still designs buildings. But she told me, her voice flat, that she no longer believes in the spaces she creates. She said, "I used to think architecture was about shelter. Now I know it's just a box. We're all just boxes waiting to be broken."

She laughed when she said it, a hollow sound. Then she went quiet. She looked at her hands, the same hands that held the steering wheel, and she did not speak again until the end of the session.
